bib.title: The Data Warehouse Toolkit, Chapter 5: Order Management
bib.venue: book chapter (The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 2nd ed., Wiley); edition and year not printed in the chapter text, taken from the caller

question: How do you dimensionally model the order management processes (orders, invoices, order fulfillment pipeline), and how do the three fact table types differ?
contributions: Order transaction and invoice transaction schemas with the design issues they raise (role-playing dates, junk dimensions, currencies, units of measure, header/line granularity).
The accumulating snapshot for the order fulfillment pipeline, with lag calculations.
A comparison of transaction, periodic snapshot and accumulating snapshot fact tables (Table 5.1).
Real-time partitions for each fact table type.

results.claim: Normalizing four facts into a generic amount plus a fact-type dimension multiplies a 10-million-row order line table to 40 million rows.
results.metric: fact table rows after fact normalization
results.setup: Order line fact table with six keys and four facts per row; normalized to seven keys and one fact per row.

results.claim: A junk dimension of 10 two-value indicators has at most 1,024 rows.
results.setup: 10 two-value flags removed from the order fact table into one junk dimension (2^10).
results.quote: you would have 1,024 (210) rows in this junk dimension
results.note: Exponent printed as 210 because superscript is flattened in the text.

results.claim: Five indicators of three values each give a 243-row junk dimension, so one junk dimension is the best route.
Five uncorrelated indicators with 100 values each give 100 million combinations, so separate dimensions are suggested.
results.quote: you now have 100 million (1005) possible combinations

results.claim: Storing 10 quantity facts plus 4 unit-of-measure conversion factors needs 14 facts per row, against 50 if every fact were stored in all 5 units.
results.setup: Orders pipeline fact table, 10 base quantity facts, 5 units of measure (one is the base unit, so 4 factors).

results.claim: A transaction grain real-time partition for a retailer with 10 million transactions a day holds about 400 MB per day, about 150 GB a year in the static table.
results.setup: 10 million transactions per day, 40-byte record (7 dimensions plus 3 facts, 4-byte fields).
results.quote: we accumulate 400 MB of data each day
results.note: Annual figure printed as 'about 150 GB of raw data'.

results.claim: A bank periodic snapshot of 15 million accounts over 36 months has 540 million rows; its real-time partition is 480 MB.
results.setup: Grain account by month, 15 million accounts, 36 months; real-time partition with 4 dimensions and 4 facts.
results.note: Partition size printed as 'a real-time partition of 480 MB'.

results.claim: An accumulating snapshot real-time partition for a manufacturer is about 600 kB (7,500 updated line items a day at 80 bytes).
results.setup: 60,000 shipment invoices/month, 20 line items each, 2-month lifetime, 5 updates per line, 80-byte records.
results.quote: 7,500 updated line items per day x 80 bytes
results.note: Also printed: 'about 7,500 line items updated on an average working day'.

results.claim: An accumulating snapshot revisits and updates fact rows, unlike transaction and periodic snapshot tables, which are insert-only.
results.setup: Table 5.1 comparison of fact table types.

results.claim: Facts of different grain (order vs order line) must not be mixed in one fact table; allocate header facts to the line, or make two tables.
results.setup: Header-level facts such as shipping charges.

limits: Chapter text only; no empirical evaluation, all numbers are illustrative worked examples.
Written 2002: real-time partitions pinned in memory with B-tree indexes, ETL and 'aggregate navigator' reflect early-2000s warehouse DBMSs; modern columnar/lakehouse engines change the trade-offs.
Authors concede profitability P&L is hard in practice because cost facts often cannot be captured at invoice line grain (p.127).
Authors say the accumulating snapshot fits short-lived processes with a definite beginning and end; long-lived ones such as bank accounts suit periodic snapshots (p.130).
Edition and year are not printed in the extracted text; 2nd ed. 2002 comes from the caller.
practices: Declare grain first: order fact table is one row per order line item (Order Transactions, p.109).
Keep facts as columns in one row rather than a generic amount plus a fact-type dimension, unless facts are sparse and no arithmetic is done between them (Fact Normalization, p.109-110).
Role-play the date dimension with one physical table and separately labeled views, one per date role (p.110-111).
Flatten product hierarchies into one denormalized dimension; do not snowflake (p.111-112).
Replace operational product keys with surrogate keys and replace cryptic codes with readable text (p.112).
Keep order number as a degenerate dimension rather than building an order-header dimension (p.117).
Pack low-cardinality flags and indicators into a junk dimension; build rows at extract time when the theoretical combinations are too many (p.117-119).
Store both local-currency and standard-currency facts, add a currency dimension, and add a daily currency-conversion fact table for any-to-any reporting (p.119-121).
Allocate header-level facts down to the line item; do not mix grains in one fact table (p.121-122).
Start a data warehouse with invoices where the company ships or bills (p.123).
Store extended (additive) dollar amounts, not unit prices, and compute averages as sum of extended price over sum of quantity (p.124-125).
Assess source cost data before promising a P&L mart; each cost fact may need its own extract (p.127).
Use an accumulating snapshot, one row per order line, with a surrogate key for each milestone date so unknown dates can be loaded as 'Unknown'/'To be determined' (p.129).
Provide lag measures as view columns computed from date differences (p.130).
Put unit-of-measure conversion factors in the fact table row and expose converted facts through views (p.131-132).
Use companion transaction and snapshot fact tables; the three types share conformed dimensions (p.132-135).
Build a lightly indexed real-time partition of the same structure as the static fact table and drill across to it (p.136-139).

terms.definition: Role-playing in a data warehouse occurs when a single dimension simultaneously appears several times in the same fact table. The underlying dimension may exist as a single physical table, but each of the roles should be presented to the data access tools in a separately labeled view.
An operational transaction identifier (e.g. order number) left in the fact table without joining to a dimension table.
A junk dimension is a convenient grouping of typically low-cardinality flags and indicators.
Flattening the parent-child relationship so facts captured at header level are spread down to the child line-item level; the same thing as activity-based costing.
A fact table with one row per lowest level of detail entering the pipeline, with multiple milestone date keys, whose rows are revisited and updated as activity happens.
A picture of activity taken at the end of a day, week or month, with the snapshots stacked consecutively in the fact table.
One row per transaction event at an instantaneous point in time; once posted, typically not revisited.
Extended net invoice less manufacturing, storage and distribution costs; not true company profit because general and administrative expenses are excluded.
A separate table, physically and administratively separate from the static warehouse tables, holding activity since the last static load, lightly indexed so data can be dribbled in.
Used here for sales rep coverage: a table recording assignments of reps to customers even when no order occurred.
